title: No greens for a week
objective: Teach a client on warfarin to keep vitamin K intake consistent, and know a higher INR means a greater bleeding risk

sources.note: Relayed from the REQ-233 NCLEX-PN cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read: Coordinated Care includes care within the legal scope of practice; Physiological Adaptation includes recognizing and reporting a change in the client's condition.

brief.situation: 16:30 in a skilled nursing facility. You are the LPN on the north hall. Mrs. Duarte, 79, on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, has an INR of 5.6 back from today's draw; last week it was 2.6. Her warfarin is due at 17:00.
handover: After dental extractions eight days ago she has been on soft foods and has eaten none of the salads and greens she usually has daily. Her daughter visits every evening.
The aide reports her gums are oozing and she had 'a dark, sticky' stool this afternoon.

Facility policy: the LPN reports an INR outside the ordered range and any bleeding to the RN supervisor and the provider at once, and may hold an anticoagulant dose pending the provider's call; the LPN reinforces teaching the RN or provider has started.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the INR means for her, what to hold, what to reinforce and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What does an INR of 5.6 mean for Mrs. Duarte, why did it rise, and what do you do within your role?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: A higher INR means slower clotting and greater bleeding risk; 5.6 is far above her range and she is bleeding (gums, bruises, black stool); it rose after her vitamin K intake fell (no greens for eight days).
parts.modelAnswer: A higher INR means her blood clots more slowly, so 5.6 means a big bleeding risk, and she's already bleeding: gums, bruises and a black stool. It went up because she stopped eating her usual greens after the dental work, so her vitamin K dropped.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Holds the warfarin pending the provider; checks vital signs and bleeding; reports to the RN supervisor and provider now; reinforces consistent vitamin K intake (not none, not a sudden large amount) and bleeding signs to report; documents.
parts.modelAnswer: Hold the warfarin, check her vital signs and for bleeding, and report to the RN supervisor and provider now. Then reinforce the teaching: steady amounts of greens week to week, not none and not a sudden big salad, and report bleeding signs.

noProgress.rationale: An INR of 5.6 with bleeding unreported an hour on is harm here.

scoring.modelReasoning: A higher INR means blood that clots more slowly and a greater bleeding risk. Mrs. Duarte's INR of 5.6 is far above her range of 2 to 3, and she is bleeding: oozing gums, bruises and a black tarry stool. It rose because her vitamin K intake fell when she stopped eating her daily greens after dental work. Within the LPN role: hold the warfarin pending the provider, check vital signs and bleeding, and report to the RN supervisor and provider now. Then reinforce the teaching: keep vitamin K foods consistent week to week (not none, and not a sudden large salad), and report black stools, bleeding gums, pink urine, headache or dizziness.

inrQ.ask: While you check: what does a higher INR mean on warfarin?

choices.label: Blood clots more slowly: a greater bleeding risk
Blood clots faster: a clot risk

inrQ.explain: Warfarin may cause serious bleeding; the INR tracks the body's response, and a higher value means slower clotting.
